title: Paint, patch and surface compatibility
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: Victorian Government, Unlicensed asbestos removal (asbestos.vic.gov.au; 'Updated' label, no date shown); WorkSafe Queensland, Asbestos licences (no date shown); SafeWork NSW, Class B asbestos removal licence (published 12 November 2025; last modified 12 March 2026); NSW Government, Painting work (last updated 23 June 2026); Queensland Building and Construction Commission, When you need a QBCC licence (last reviewed 11 August 2021); Consumer Affairs Victoria, What work requires a building contract? (last updated 25 September 2025); NSW Government, Dry plastering work (last updated 23 June 2026); NSW Government, Wet plastering work (last updated 23 June 2026).
audience: Handyman workers, painters and plasterers at the basic level
learningOutcomes: Assess a surface for condition, contamination and compatibility before painting or patching.
Choose a patch material and primer that suit the substrate and the existing finish.
Identify when older surfaces need specialist assessment before disturbance.

instruction.heading: Read the surface before you touch it
instruction.body: Before patching or painting, look at the surface in good light. Note cracks, bulging, damp, staining, flaking paint, grease, mould, and any sign of previous repairs. Test the surface by pressing it with a fingertip and by scraping a small area to see whether the paint lifts. Decide whether the surface is sound, needs cleaning, or needs specialist assessment. Damp, active staining, and any surface that is crumbling or moving are not ready for paint until the cause is known. Painting over a moisture problem hides the evidence and makes the next repair harder.

instruction.heading: Patch and prime to suit the substrate
instruction.body: Use a patch material that suits the substrate and the depth of the repair. Filler suits shallow gaps in painted surfaces; deeper repairs may need a different material. Prime bare or patched areas before finishing, and select a primer that suits the substrate and the finish: a stain-blocking primer for staining, an alkali-resistant primer for new plaster or masonry where the product label requires it, and a bonding product where the surface is glossy or smooth. Check the product label and data sheet for the surface and the conditions. A patch that has not cured or dried will show through the finish.

instruction.heading: Older surfaces, dust and licence boundaries
instruction.body: In older buildings, paint and plaster may contain lead or asbestos. Do not sand, scrape, cut or demolish older paint or plaster until its composition is confirmed by a competent specialist. Asbestos removal above a state's allowance is licensed work. In Victoria, unlicensed removal of non-friable asbestos is limited to 10 square metres in total, and to one hour in any period of seven days which is cumulative across all employees (asbestos.vic.gov.au page, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). In Queensland, non-friable jobs at or under 10 square metres need no licence (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). In New South Wales, a Class B licence applies once the area of non-friable material passes 10 square metres (SafeWork NSW page, published 12 November 2025, modified 12 March 2026). Do not apply one state's figure to another. Painting and plastering licence positions are set out in the safety and regulatory points below.

procedure: Inspect the surface in good light and note defects, damp, staining, grease and mould.
Check for loose or flaking paint and for damp before deciding to paint or patch.
Clean the surface and let it dry where cleaning is needed.
Choose a patch material for the depth and the substrate, and let it cure.
Prime the repair and any bare or stained area with a primer suited to the substrate.
If the surface may contain lead or asbestos, stop and refer for specialist assessment before disturbing it.
Record the surface condition, the products used and any unresolved defect.

workedExamples.situation: You are asked to paint a bedroom wall where a brown stain has appeared under the window after rain. The paint is flaking near the sill.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should you paint over the stain and flaking paint to finish the job?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The stain and flaking near the sill point to a moisture source that has not been found. Painting over it hides the evidence and will fail. Record the moisture, refer the cause for investigation, and only paint once the cause is known and the surface is sound and dry. The painting job can be quoted separately once the approver agrees.

equipmentAndPpe: Scraper, sanding block and cleaning cloth
Patch materials and primers suited to the substrate
Dust mask or respirator suited to the task
Drop sheets and masking for the surrounds

commonErrors.error: Painting over damp or active staining.
commonErrors.prevention: Find and record the moisture source, and paint only when the surface is dry and sound.

commonErrors.error: Using a primer that does not suit the substrate or the stain.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the product label and data sheet for the surface, and use a stain-blocking primer where staining is present.

commonErrors.error: Sanding older paint without checking for lead or asbestos.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, do not disturb the older surface, and refer for specialist assessment.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Painting licence positions. In NSW, a contractor licence is needed for painting valued above $5,000 including GST, but stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork have not needed one since 2015 unless they form part of other home building work. The same page lists a qualified supervisor certificate as a licence type for painting work (NSW painting page, last updated 23 June 2026). Queensland: painting and decorating is a QBCC licence class. The QBCC incidental work page says: “The total value of incidental work cannot be any more than $3,300 and may be included in your contract.” That page shows no date beyond its 2023 copyright line. The QBCC painting page (last reviewed 31 Aug 2021) says fees and charges were increased on 1 July 2026, so whether the $3,300 limit is current after 1 July 2026 is not confirmed by an official source. That page does not say whether painting-only work needs a licence, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point. Victoria: the Consumer Affairs Victoria page (last updated 25 September 2025) places painting on its list of trades that fall outside the higher-value written contract rule when a job involves only that trade. The Consumer Victoria registration page says “You do not have to register with the BPC for jobs that involve only one of the following:” The list includes “painting.”

Plastering licence positions. New South Wales: dry and wet plastering each need a contractor licence or qualified supervisor certificate for work priced above $5,000 across labour and materials, GST included (NSW dry plastering and wet plastering pages, both last updated 23 June 2026). Victoria: plastering is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria list of single trades that fall outside the higher-value written contract rule (CAV page, last updated 25 September 2025). A job that combines painting and plastering does not fit that single-trade list, so the written-contract rule above $10,000 may apply. The Consumer Victoria registration page says “You do not have to register with the BPC for jobs that involve only one of the following:” and its list includes “plastering.”

Asbestos thresholds differ by state, and one state's figure does not transfer to another. Victoria: unlicensed removal of non-friable material is limited to 10 square metres in total, and to one hour in any period of seven days which is cumulative across all employees (asbestos.vic.gov.au, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). Friable asbestos has no unlicensed allowance, and work above these limits needs a licence. Queensland: non-friable material at or under 10 square metres needs no licence (WorkSafe Queensland, no date shown). New South Wales: a Class B licence applies once the area of non-friable material passes 10 square metres (SafeWork NSW, published 12 November 2025, modified 12 March 2026).
Lead paint and older-surface work: refer it.
Completing this lesson does not give a painting, plastering or asbestos licence, certificate or authority.

qualityStandard: The surface is inspected and its condition recorded before any patch or paint is applied.
No paint is applied over damp or active staining without the cause being recorded.
The primer and patch material are recorded against the substrate.
documentationEvidence: Surface condition record with photos taken with consent
Product record for patch, primer and paint used
Referral note for any older surface requiring specialist assessment
summary: Read the surface and find the cause of any damp or staining before covering it.
Patch and prime to the substrate and the finish, and let the repair dry and cure.
Refer older surfaces for specialist assessment before disturbing them, and check the licence position for the state.

knowledgeChecks.question: A wall shows a brown stain under a window after rain, and the paint is flaking. What should you do?
options: Paint over it with a thick coat to hide the stain before the client sees it
Find and record the moisture source, and paint only once the surface is dry and sound
Sand it and paint the same day, while the surface is still warm from the sun
Use the cheapest paint to cover it, since the stain will not show through

knowledgeChecks.question: An older building has painted surfaces that may contain lead. What should happen before sanding?
options: Sand it with a mask on, since the mask keeps the dust out of the lungs
Sand it wet to reduce dust, so the paint comes off more cleanly
Stop, do not disturb the surface, and refer for specialist assessment
Remove the paint with a heat gun, since heat loosens the layers quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about Victorian asbestos removal is supported by the source?
options: Unlicensed removal of any amount is allowed, provided the worker wears a mask, gloves and disposable overalls throughout the whole job
Unlicensed removal of friable asbestos is allowed up to 10 square metres, provided the material is wet and bagged on site
The source gives no limits on the amount of asbestos that an unlicensed worker may remove from any building in the state at all
Unlicensed removal of non-friable asbestos is allowed up to 10 square metres in total, and up to one hour in any period of seven days
